questions.q: You already know SQL joins from T-SQL Development. Which Tableau feature behaves exactly like a SQL JOIN?
options: A Tableau join, built inside a logical table's physical layer — you pick a join type and matching fields, and rows combine immediately
A Tableau relationship — it's identical to a SQL JOIN
A calculated field
A dashboard filter action
questions.explain: A Tableau join (inside the physical layer) is conceptually identical to a SQL JOIN — pick a join type, pick matching fields, rows combine immediately. A relationship is Tableau's own different mechanism.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a relationship and a join in terms of when rows get combined?
options: A join combines rows immediately, up front; a relationship waits and only combines what a given worksheet actually needs, at the level of detail that worksheet needs
There is no difference — both combine rows at the same time
A relationship always combines rows before a join does
Joins never combine rows until you build a dashboard
questions.explain: Joins fix the combine immediately, like SQL. Relationships are context-aware — Tableau defers combining data until a worksheet references fields from both tables, at that worksheet's level of detail.

questions.q: Do you pick a join type (inner/left/right/full outer) when creating a relationship?
options: No — relationships don't have a join-type picker; Tableau handles that automatically per worksheet
Yes, it's required before you can drag a second table onto the canvas
Only if you're using a live connection, not an extract
Yes, but only for cross-database relationships
questions.explain: The relationship canvas asks only which fields match — no join-type dropdown. That's one of the concrete differences from a join, which does require picking a type.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should you still reach for an actual join instead of a relationship?
options: When you need a non-equality condition (like < or >=), an intentional row-duplication setup for row-level security, or a single flat combined result for performance reasons
Never — relationships can do everything a join can do
Only when connecting to Excel files
Only when using Tableau Public instead of Tableau Desktop
questions.explain: Relationships cover most everyday analysis, but non-equality join conditions, certain row-level-security patterns, and cases needing one flat combined table still call for a real join.

questions.q: What is the 'noodle' in Tableau's data modeling terminology?
options: The line drawn between two logical tables on the relationship canvas, representing their relationship
A calculated field that returns a string
The icon used to represent a union
A nickname for the Data pane
questions.explain: The noodle is the connecting line between logical tables on the relationship canvas — click or right-click it to open Edit Relationship.
